text:
Alfred North Whitehead was an English mathematician and philosopher, born in Ramsgate, Kent, in 1861. He studied mathematics at Trinity College, Cambridge, where he earned his B.A. in 1884 and excelled in mathematics. He taught and wrote on mathematics and physics at Cambridge until 1910, during which time he collaborated with Bertrand Russell on *Principia Mathematica* (1910–1913).
Moving to the United States in 1924 to teach philosophy at Harvard University, Whitehead made significant philosophical contributions. He wrote *Science and the Modern World* (1925), which challenged Cartesian dualism, and *Process and Reality* (1929). His philosophy, known as "process philosophy," rejected the notion of irreducible brute matter, advocating instead for an event-based ontology where all entities are interrelated processes. Whitehead also developed the term "prehension" to describe perception, applicable to both conscious and unconscious entities.
